title: The Holy Innocents (28 December)
hookLine: the children killed by Herod; a day for all suffering children

cards: Not every Christmas carol is cheerful. There's an old English one, a lullaby, sung in the voice of the mothers of Bethlehem, rocking their babies and knowing what's coming. Gentle and terrible at once.
A few days after Christmas, the church calendar stops the celebration and remembers something nobody would put on a greeting card: the children of Bethlehem killed on the orders of a frightened king.
In some churches the vestments turn red, the color worn for martyrs, and in some it has become a day to pray for every child who suffers.

teach.b: Matthew tells it. Wise men from the east come to King Herod asking where the newborn king of the Jews is. Herod is alarmed.
He sends them on to Bethlehem and asks them to report back. They find the child and, warned in a dream, go home another way. Herod "saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth."
He orders the children of Bethlehem killed. Joseph, warned in a dream too, has already fled with Mary and the child into Egypt.

teach.h: THE CHILD ESCAPES; THE OTHERS DON'T.
teach.b: The child escapes. The others don't.

Matthew reaches back to the prophet Jeremiah: "In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not."
Rachel is one of the mothers of Israel, Jacob's beloved wife, and Genesis says she was buried near this very town: "And Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem."
So Matthew pictures the old mother crying from her grave over the children of her own town.
Would not be comforted. The text doesn't hurry her, or explain the deaths, or tidy them up. It lets her grief stand.
Tradition calls the Holy Innocents holy not because of anything they did, but because they died, children, in the shadow of the story of Jesus.
So the day reaches out to every child caught in someone else's fear and violence, in war, in hunger, in harm at home. Rachel is still weeping, and the day asks the church to weep with her.

how: Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches keep the Holy Innocents a few days after Christmas, and the Orthodox remember them on their own calendar; some churches use the day to pray for children who suffer, and some bless children at the service.

games.q: you're Joseph. in a dream, you're warned that Herod will seek the child. what do you do?
o: take Mary and the child and flee into Egypt.
go to Herod and plead for the child.
games.why: Joseph takes the family into Egypt by night. the child escapes — and Matthew does not look away from the children who don't.

practice: Let one suffering child have your attention: a face from the news, a child you know who's having a hard time, or the children of one troubled place.

Don't rush to fix the feeling; let it be heavy for a moment, the way Rachel's grief is allowed to be. If you pray, you can hold those children before God; if you don't, simply hold them in mind, and stay with them.

wordCard.voice: Herod. The frightened king whose orders killed the children of Bethlehem, remembered on this quiet day just after Christmas.

orig.note: Hebrew: Rachel — one of the mothers of Israel in Genesis, weeping for her children in Jeremiah 31:15.
